# Executive summary {-}

This report consolidates a close reading of the three leading "ambient-aware" guide-assignment
methods — **geomux**, **fishash**, and **CLEANSER** — against the datasets they analyzed, their
conclusions, and our own cross-dataset measurements, and ends with a re-analysis of why CLEANSER
appeared to fail on our SCEPTRE3 simulations.

**Bottom line / recommendation.** Grounded in real barnyard ground truth and FDR experiments across
Simpson $\times$ overdispersion $\times$ MOI regimes: **adopt fishash's contingency core (Fisher test +
Simpson correction + Guo–Sarkar FDR), plus one canonical improvement of our own — decontaminate the
*cell* margin (use ambient depth, not library size).** fishash decontaminates the guide margin but uses
the raw, signal-contaminated library size as each cell's ambient exposure; our cross-dataset work shows
that's wrong, and the symmetric fix **beats fishash at MOI ≥ 1 (it recovers the recall fishash loses)
while tying at low MOI and on real barnyard, at controlled FDR.** It targets fishash's *documented*
high-MOI weak spot. Two from-scratch alternatives were tested and rejected: a marginal NB method (it is
*dominated* — conditioning beats marginal), and an overdispersion tail (works on sims but its φ is not
robustly estimable on real data — keep fishash's hypergeometric). The simple ambient test stays as a
fast high-signal default, but it is not FDR-calibrated and is not the flagship.

**Five supporting takeaways:**

1. **All three are the same idea with different machinery.** Each assigns guide *g* to cell *c*
   when its UMI count exceeds an **ambient null** whose mean factorizes as
   $\lambda_{g,c} = \gamma_g \cdot \kappa_c$ — a *guide ambient share* $\gamma_g$ times a *cell
   ambient depth* $\kappa_c$. geomux and fishash test against this null with a Fisher/hypergeometric
   test (contingency-table view); CLEANSER fits it as a per-guide Bayesian negative-binomial
   mixture. Our ambient-proportion test is the shared statistical core.

2. **fishash is the current state of the art on real ground truth** — the only method strong on
   *both* CROP-seq and direct-capture barnyard data — because it adds two corrections to the plain
   test: a **Simpson's-paradox correction** (cell/guide-margin contamination) and a
   **block-dependent FDR correction**. We reproduced its Simpson phenomenon exactly.

3. **geomux = our ambient test + a heuristic log-odds threshold.** It is fast and well-calibrated at
   low MOI but its published benchmark is thin (simulation-only, one competitor) and it **collapses
   on direct-capture** data (it stops assigning).

4. **CLEANSER's distinctive contributions are empirical and on-target for us**: it is built on an
   experimentally-validated ambient characterization, it **normalizes per-cell depth** with exactly
   our $\kappa_c$ (the sub-threshold UMI sum), and it **models overdispersion** (NB ambient for
   direct-capture). Its costs are MCMC runtime, per-guide independence (no cross-guide sharing of the
   ambient pool), and heavy prior dependence.

5. **CLEANSER did *not* underperform on our SCEPTRE3 sims — the benchmark mis-scored it.** The
   scoring function counted *every* guide–cell pair CLEANSER emitted a posterior for as a positive
   assignment, never applying the posterior threshold. Re-scoring the *same* output files at the
   standard 0.5 cutoff turns its reported Jaccard of **0.43 → 0.89** (precision 0.99). This is a
   one-line fix in our analysis code, not a flaw in CLEANSER.

---

# The unifying framework

Treat the gRNA count matrix as $N_{g,c}$ = UMIs of guide $g$ in cell $c$, with margins
$N_{g,\cdot}$ (guide total), $N_{\cdot,c}$ (cell total / library size), $N$ (grand total). Assignment
asks, for each pair, whether $N_{g,c}$ is **larger than ambient contamination alone would produce**.

The ambient (noise) process is, to first order, a **rank-1 Poisson field**:

$$\mathbb{E}\big[N^{\text{noise}}_{g,c}\big] \;=\; \gamma_g \cdot \kappa_c,
\qquad \textstyle\sum_g \gamma_g = 1,$$

where $\gamma_g$ is guide $g$'s **share of the ambient pool** (a single composition vector) and
$\kappa_c$ is cell $c$'s **ambient capture depth**. Everything below is a different way to (a) estimate
this rank-1 field and (b) test a count against it.

| | how it estimates $\gamma_g$ | how it estimates $\kappa_c$ | the test | extra machinery |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **simple per-guide threshold** (Otsu, valley) | — (ignores guides jointly) | — (ignores cell depth) | per-guide bimodal cut on log counts | none |
| **ambient test** (ours) | global share $N_{g,\cdot}/N$ | library size $N_{\cdot,c}$ | one-sided Poisson/hypergeometric, BH | one knob (FDR $q$) |
| **geomux** | guide margin $N_{g,\cdot}$ | cell margin $N_{\cdot,c}$ | one-sided hypergeometric, BH | adaptive **log-odds-ratio** per-cell gate |
| **fishash** | **noise-only** profile (rank-1 Poisson completion) | column margin $N_{\cdot,c}$ | hypergeometric on the noise-conditioned table | **Simpson correction** + **Guo–Sarkar block FDR** |
| **CLEANSER** | per-guide fitted rate $\lambda_j$ / $\mu_{j,\text{noise}}$ | $L_i$ = sub-threshold UMI sum | per-guide **NB mixture**, MCMC posterior | overdispersion ($\phi$), Bayesian priors |

The spectrum runs **simple test → contingency table (geomux, fishash) → mixture model (CLEANSER)**.
geomux and fishash sit at the same node; fishash is strictly more sophisticated (geomux adds only a
threshold; fishash adds two principled corrections). CLEANSER is the generative pole — it models both
the noise *and* the signal distribution per guide, buying overdispersion-robustness at the price of
MCMC and per-guide independence.

---

# The three methods in depth

## geomux — contingency test + a log-odds gate

**Source.** Teyssier (2024), UCSF PhD dissertation, Ch. 5; code `noamteyssier/geomux` (v0.5.5);
simulator `muxsim`. The geomux *method* chapter is **simulation-only**.

**Model.** On a cell×guide matrix, after QC ($\geq 5$ UMI per cell/guide), each count is tested under
a hypergeometric null parameterized by the table margins,
$N_{g,c}\sim\text{Hypergeometric}(N,\,N_{\cdot,c},\,N_{g,\cdot})$ — i.e. exactly the rank-1 ambient
null with $\gamma_g = N_{g,\cdot}/N$, $\kappa_c = N_{\cdot,c}$. P-values are BH-adjusted. The **only**
addition beyond the ambient test is a per-cell **log-odds-ratio gate**: guides are sorted by adjusted
p-value and iteratively demoted to "noise" if their logit gap to the most-significant insignificant
guide falls below a threshold $T_L$ (fixed $=1$ in the dissertation; *adaptive* in current code, an
undocumented `adaptive_lor_scalar`). No block FDR, no overdispersion, no doublet model.

**Datasets.** None real in the method chapter — 3,456 parameter combinations of `muxsim` multinomial
simulations with an **equiprobable** ambient background (unrealistic). Real applications appear only
in other chapters (dementia CROP-seq screen, **GSE207099**; an ASD CROP-seq screen, accession not
stated).

**Benchmark.** A single competitor — **demuxEM** (a cell-hashing demultiplexer, not a guide-assignment
SOTA) — on MOI-level metrics (accuracy = fraction of cells with correctly predicted MOI). geomux beats
demuxEM at MOI $\leq 2$ and is ~10× faster; demuxEM wins at MOI $> 2$ (author-stated).

**Right.** Statistically motivated, interpretable, few knobs; conditions on both margins (the two
first-order ambient effects); excellent FDR control and speed; the log-odds gate is a sensible
per-cell signal-to-noise filter.

**Wrong / limits.** Benchmark is thin (one non-comparable competitor, simulation-only, MOI-level
metrics, no per-guide precision/recall, no comparison to crispat/CLEANSER/sceptre/fishash). The
equiprobable-background simulator flatters it. The **pooled signal+noise null makes it the
*uncorrected* Simpson curve** (see §[Simpson]). On real barnyard data it **collapses on
direct-capture** (it assigns nothing in many cells — accuracy 0.75/0.53; fishash Table 2). The
threshold is not principled in the paper.

## fishash — the corrected contingency method (current SOTA)

**Source.** Kamm, Yeung & Forrest (2026), bioRxiv 2026.01.22.701179; package `jackkamm/fishash`
(v0.99.0). Defaults: `padj_method="GS"`, `refit=10`.

**Model.** A one-sided Fisher/hypergeometric test per $(g,c)$, plus two corrections:

- **Simpson's-paradox correction.** The plain test pools signal and noise; for a low-signal guide this
  can flip the $2\times2$ odds ratio above 1 even when the guide is truly absent (Prop. 1, Fig. 2).
  fishash replaces the "other-cells" counts with **noise-only** counts (adjusted odds ratio $R^*$,
  Eq. 7), estimating the latent noise counts by **rank-1 Poisson matrix completion** of the
  assigned-masked matrix (Eq. 9), iterated with a mask schedule (Alg. 1). This is a direct, transparent
  estimate of the rank-1 ambient field $\gamma_g\kappa_c$ from the noise.
- **Guo–Sarkar (2020) block FDR.** Because hypergeometric components within a cell are *negatively*
  associated (violating BH's PRDS), fishash uses a per-cell block correction, not plain BH.

`fishash(refit=0)` = the plain Fisher test = geomux's core = our ambient test.

**Datasets.** (i) **Barnyard** (Liu 2025, **GSE272457**) — species-mixing CROP-seq + direct-capture,
the canonical real ground truth (Table 2). (ii) **Replogle 2022** genome-wide K562 (figshare 20127869),
with a *proxy* truth (paired dual-guide co-occurrence). (iii) A **CellBender-based simulator**
(`guidebender`) sweeping #guides (Fig. 5), MOI (Fig. 6), and signal–noise correlation (Fig. 7,
Simpson). The bundled Schraivogel object is only a package test fixture, **not** used in the figures.

**Benchmark (the most complete in the field).** Comparators: CLEANSER, crispat (4 mixtures), DemuxEM,
**geomux 0.5.5**, SCEPTRE. Headline numbers:

- **Barnyard Table 2** (CROP-0hr / CROP-72hr / DC-0hr / DC-72hr): fishash
  **0.956 / 0.953 / 0.910 / 0.949** — only method strong on all four. geomux wins CROP-seq narrowly
  (0.958 / 0.956) but **collapses on DC (0.747 / 0.525)**. crispat-PoissonGauss ~0.95 (CROP only).
- **Replogle proxy**: fishash highest F1 in **78%** of 273 runs, highest recall (median 97%); but
  **no method exceeds ~71% precision** (proxy-truth ceiling from promoter silencing).
- **Sims (Fig. 5)**: fishash controls FDR (precision $\geq 0.95$) in **all 100** simulations; geomux
  **fails nominal FDR**, especially in the low-expression regime.
- **Sims (Fig. 6, MOI)**: fishash best for MOI $\leq 0.5$; **dcCLEANSER best for $1 \leq$ MOI $\leq 3$**;
  crispat-PoissonGauss best for MOI $\geq 5$. No method dominates everywhere.
- **Resources (Fig. 8)**: fishash & geomux are the cheapest (seconds, <1 GiB) even at 80,000 guides.

**Right.** Best real-data accuracy across chemistries; reproducible FDR control; the Simpson correction
removes false positives *without* costing recall (we reproduced this — §[Simpson]); excellent
scalability; unusually honest reporting (publishes where competitors win).

**Wrong / limits (mostly stated).** The hypergeometric core assumes **conditional equidispersion**;
under overdispersed noise the authors' own Appendix C shows fishash **loses FDR control** — and
direct-capture ambient is overdispersed (CLEANSER's finding). The method is iterative with a
hand-tuned mask schedule; the noise model is rank-1 while their generative model is rank-2 (an
acknowledged estimator/model mismatch); and there is **no fully-known-truth real dataset** (barnyard is
high-signal cell lines; Replogle truth is a proxy).

## CLEANSER — the validated mixture model

**Source.** Liu, Hamilton et al. (2025), *Cell Genomics* 5:100766; repo
`Gersbachlab-Bioinformatics/CLEANSER`.

**Empirical foundation (its real contribution).** A human/mouse dCas9-KRAB **barnyard** screen
(MOI ~10) with species-specific non-targeting libraries gives *provable* ambient labels (a guide in the
wrong species is ambient). Findings: ambient is **droplet/prep-borne, not co-culture exchange**;
ambient UMIs correlate with native UMIs; transduced-vs-ambient separation is **7–13× for CROP-seq** but
**50–266× for direct-capture**; and — the modeling crux — **CROP-seq ambient is ~Poisson but
direct-capture ambient is overdispersed (NB)**.

**Model.** A per-guide, zero-truncated two-component mixture fit by Stan MCMC:

- **csCLEANSER (CROP-seq):** $X_i \sim (1-r)\,\text{Poisson}(\lambda) + r\,\text{NB}(\mu,\phi)$.
- **dcCLEANSER (direct-capture):** $X_i \sim (1-r)\,\text{NB}(\mu_0,\phi_0) + r\,\text{NB}(\mu_1,\phi_1)$.

with a hard constraint $\mu_{\text{signal}} > \lambda_{\text{noise}}$, a strong $r\sim\text{Beta}(1,10)$
prior (most pairs are ambient), and a **cell normalization $L_i$** = the cell's sum of gRNA UMIs $\leq 2$,
normalized to mean 1; means scale as $\lambda_{ij} = \lambda_j L_i$, $\mu_{ij} = \mu_j L_i$. Output is
the **posterior** $P(\text{native} \mid X_i)$ per pair; assignment thresholds it (defaults 0.8 CROP-seq,
0.5 direct-capture).

**This is our framework, generatively.** $L_i$ **is** our cell depth $\kappa_c$ (the sub-threshold UMI
sum); $\lambda_j$ / $\mu_{j,\text{noise}}$ plays the role of $\gamma_g$ (the guide ambient rate) — but
**fitted independently per guide**, losing the rank-1 cross-guide tie. csCLEANSER's Poisson ambient
$\lambda_j L_i$ is *exactly* our ambient mean $\gamma_g\kappa_c$; dcCLEANSER generalizes it to NB — the
one thing a rank-1 Poisson null cannot do.

**Datasets.** Its own barnyard (**GSE272457**, have it); reprocessed **Gasperini 2019** (GSE120861,
BAM-only); **McCutcheon 2023** CD8 T-cell direct-capture (**GSE218988**); **Chardon 2023** K562 CRISPRa
direct-capture (processed matrices on washington.edu).

**Benchmark.** Versus a strict UMI cutoff and the **10X Mixture Model** only (no SCEPTRE/geomux/fishash).
Validation is **indirect** — downstream DE hits + small-*n* RT-qPCR, and "% non-transduced retained" on
the barnyard — rather than a precision/recall table. Claims 32 extra CRISPRa hits vs the 10X model, 4/6
unique hits qPCR-validated.

**Right.** Empirically-grounded **depth normalization** ($L_i\!=\!\kappa_c$, validated against ambient
load); **data-driven overdispersion** (Poisson vs NB by platform); the only method *trained* on known
ambient; open and editable; soft-probability output.

**Wrong / limits.** **MCMC cost** (per-guide Stan; zero-truncation was needed just for tractability —
poor fit for genome scale); **per-guide independence** (no shared ambient pool, the central contrast
with the contingency view); **no Simpson/contingency correction**; **heavy prior dependence** tuned to
HEK293T/NIH3T3 at MOI 10 (on the low-UMI T-cell data the posterior cutoff had to be hand-dropped to
0.08); a **fixed $\leq 2$** normalization threshold; weak validation (no head-to-head accuracy table on
the ground truth it generated).

# Head-to-head: what each gets right and wrong

| dimension | geomux | fishash | CLEANSER |
|---|---|---|---|
| statistical core | hypergeometric test | hypergeometric test | NB mixture (MCMC) |
| per-cell depth $\kappa_c$ | column margin (implicit) | column margin (implicit) | **explicit $L_i$ = sub-threshold sum** |
| per-guide ambient $\gamma_g$ | row margin (pooled) | **noise-only, rank-1 completion** | per-guide fit (no sharing) |
| Simpson/contamination | ✗ (uncorrected) | ✔ correction | ✗ |
| overdispersion | ✗ | ✗ (equidispersed; fails in App. C) | ✔ **NB ambient** |
| multiple testing | BH | **Guo–Sarkar block** | Bayesian posterior |
| real ground-truth accuracy | CROP-seq good, **DC collapses** | **best on both chemistries** | not tabulated vs truth |
| speed / scale | **excellent** | **excellent** | poor (MCMC) |
| principal weakness | thin benchmark, no DC, uncorrected | overdispersion (App. C) | cost, priors, per-guide |

**The cleanest synthesis:** fishash and CLEANSER address **orthogonal** failure modes of the plain
test. fishash fixes the **mean** (Simpson contamination of the rank-1 field) but keeps an equidispersed
tail; CLEANSER fixes the **variance** (NB overdispersion) but keeps a contaminated, per-guide mean and
no contingency correction. Neither fixes both. geomux fixes neither (it is the plain test plus a
threshold). A method that estimated a **decontaminated rank-1 ambient field** *and* used an
**overdispersion-robust (or nonparametric) tail** would dominate both — this is the design target.

---

# Our cross-dataset empirical findings

We measured the two halves of the ambient field — depth $\kappa_c$ and composition $\gamma_g$ — across
**17 real datasets** (10 perturb-seq survey datasets, Gasperini, Replogle, Schraivogel, 4 barnyard
samples). The picture both supports and sharpens the methods above.

![Ambient depth & composition across 17 real datasets. (A) Library size overstates ambient depth in
every dataset (median 51×, up to 424×). (B) The decoupling is worst at low MOI. (C) The ambient pool is
uneven everywhere (Gini median 0.43). (D) CLEANSER's cheap sub-threshold depth tracks the true ambient
depth — except on very deep direct-capture data, where the fixed ≤2 threshold breaks.](results/ambient_intuition/survey.png)

**Depth is not library size — universally.** A cell's gRNA library is ~89–100% its own real
integration, so naive library size overstates ambient depth by a **median 51× (range 2.7–424×)** and is
nearly uncorrelated with it at low MOI (Panel A–B). This is exactly why **CLEANSER's $L_i$ and fishash's
column-margin normalization matter**, and why a plain count threshold fails. CLEANSER's sub-threshold
estimator recovers the true ambient depth well (median $r=0.81$) **except on very deep direct-capture**
(its fixed $\leq 2$ threshold misses ambient when counts routinely exceed 2 — Panel D), arguing for a
*depth-adaptive* threshold.

![Per guide, all-UMI share vs ambient share. The naive global composition is an excellent proxy for the
ambient composition in small libraries (100% of guides within 2×) but degrades in large complex
libraries (iPSC: only 63% within 2×).](results/ambient_intuition/guide_margin.png)

**Composition is uneven, and its contamination scales with library complexity.** The ambient pool spans
~10–40× across guides (Gini median 0.43; Panel C). The naive global share is an unbiased proxy for the
true ambient share on average, but its *variance* grows with library size — in an 86-guide screen 100%
of guides agree within 2×, in a 6800-guide iPSC library only 63% do. This is the guide-margin Simpson
contamination fishash corrects and geomux/CLEANSER do not.

**We reproduced fishash's Simpson phenomenon** (Fig. 7) using its own simulator and package: the
uncorrected test (= our ambient core) inflates FDR to ~0.20 and fails the nominal 5% in 10/10 reps when
ambient composition is uncorrelated with signal; the correction restores FDR to 0.003 with unchanged
recall.

![Reproducing fishash's Simpson's-paradox correction (their Fig. 7) with the real package: uncorrected
(plain Fisher = our ambient core) vs corrected.](results/simpson_paradox_repro.png)

# CLEANSER on our SCEPTRE3 sims: the "underperformance" is a scoring artifact

**The reported result.** In our lab benchmark (`assignment-writeup.Rmd`), CLEANSER on the
`replogle-rd7_simulated` sims looked dramatically worse than SCEPTRE/crispat:

| sim | method | Jaccard | precision | recall |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.5% Pert (25 guides) | SCEPTRE | 0.93 | 0.96 | 0.97 |
| 1.5% Pert (25 guides) | crispat | 0.95 | 0.98 | 0.97 |
| 1.5% Pert (25 guides) | **CLEANSER** | **0.43** | **0.43** | 0.995 |
| 0.5% Pert (10 guides) | **CLEANSER** | **0.22** | **0.22** | 0.997 |

The signature — precision $\approx$ Jaccard, recall $\approx 1$ — is **pure over-assignment**: CLEANSER
appears to call almost everything.

**The diagnosis.** The over-assignment is an artifact of how the benchmark *read* CLEANSER's output,
not of CLEANSER. The runner `run_cleanser.py` writes a posterior for **every** guide–cell pair with a
nonzero count (the zero-truncated model conditions on count $> 0$). The scoring function then does:

```r
process_clns <- function(clns_output_fp, assn_list, ground_truth) {
  clns_assign_raw <- read.csv(clns_output_fp)
  unordered_cell_list <- split(clns_assign_raw$cell_id, clns_assign_raw$grna_id)  # <- takes ALL cells
  ...                                                                              # <- never filters on `posterior`
}
```

It takes **every** `cell_id` in the file as an assignment — it never thresholds `posterior`. So
CLEANSER's output is collapsed to "assign if count $\geq 1$." (Tellingly, the *commented-out*
`process_clns_parts` did threshold at `posterior > 0.8`; the active path dropped it.)

**The proof.** The arithmetic matches exactly: the output file has 83,851 recorded pairs, the sim has
36,418 true perturbations, and $36418 / 83851 = 0.434$ = the reported "precision." Re-scoring the
**same** CLEANSER output file at the standard **0.5 posterior threshold**:

| | reported (no threshold) | re-scored (posterior > 0.5) |
|---|---|---|
| 1.5% Pert | precision 0.43, Jaccard 0.43 | **precision 0.988, recall 0.903, Jaccard 0.893** |

CLEANSER's false positives at the 0.5 cutoff are a small number of genuine ambient-tail cells (median
raw count 5, all $\geq 3$), and it correctly rejects the large majority of them. **At the standard
threshold CLEANSER is competitive with SCEPTRE and crispat on these sims.**

**The corrected benchmark.** Re-scoring the **same** CLEANSER output files at the proper threshold
(0.5 for `--dc`), per-guide, reproduces the writeup's buggy numbers exactly when un-thresholded
(validating the scorer) and gives the corrected result:

| sim | SCEPTRE | crispat | pertpy | CLEANSER (buggy) | **CLEANSER (fixed)** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1.5% pert, 25 guides | 0.93 | 0.96 | 0.08 | 0.43 | **0.89** |
| 0.5% pert, 10 guides | 0.93 | 0.95 | 0.11 | 0.22 | **0.95** |

(Jaccard; `results/benchmark_update/cleanser_corrected.csv`.) Corrected CLEANSER is competitive with
SCEPTRE and crispat — it *ties* crispat on the 0.5%-pert sim. Its real cost is **runtime** (~14–50 min
MCMC vs SCEPTRE's 0.2 min). The "CLEANSER underperforms" conclusion was a one-line scoring bug, not a
property of CLEANSER.

| dataset | paper(s) | platform | accession | status |

| Gasperini 2019 K562 | CLEANSER | CROP-seq | GSE120861 | refs/sims locally; raw is BAM-only |
| Replogle 2022 genome-wide | fishash | CROP-seq | figshare 20127869 | refs/sims locally; full set is genome-scale |
| Schraivogel (TAP-seq) | (fishash fixture only) | CROP-seq | via crispat | **have** (`crispat_schraivogel`) |
| McCutcheon 2023 CD8 T-cell | CLEANSER | **direct-capture** | GSE218988 | **✔ downloaded + added** (40 guides × 22,100 cells) |
| Chardon 2023 K562 CRISPRa | CLEANSER | **direct-capture** | washington.edu | not yet; processed matrices available |

**Action taken.** We downloaded the most valuable genuinely-missing, feasibly-downloadable dataset:
**McCutcheon 2023 (GSE218988)** — a **direct-capture** CD8 T-cell CRISPRi screen that CLEANSER used and
where it was most fragile. A CRISPRi donor's processed CellRanger output (~382 MB) was pulled and the
CRISPR-Guide-Capture submatrix extracted to
`~/data/external/mccutcheon-2023-GSE218988/grna_matrix.rds` (**40 guides × 22,100 cells, median library
just 8 UMIs** — confirming the very-low-UMI direct-capture regime where CLEANSER needed a hand-dropped
0.08 cutoff). This is exactly where our analysis predicts overdispersion matters most, and we held few
such datasets; it is ready to fold into the cross-dataset depth/composition sweep. (geomux's GSE207099
exposes only assignment tables, not count matrices; Gasperini/Replogle full raw sets require CellRanger
reprocessing and we already hold calibrated references/sims; the Chardon CRISPRa matrices remain an easy
future add.)

# Build vs. adopt: an experimental test

The analysis above suggested an opening: a method fixing **both** failure modes — a decontaminated
rank-1 ambient mean (fishash's strength) **and** an overdispersion-robust tail (CLEANSER's strength) —
as a fast closed-form test. I implemented exactly that candidate
(`scripts/ambient_nb_method.R`): estimate $\gamma_g\kappa_c$ from noise-masked margins (the mean fix),
then test each count against $\text{NB}(\gamma_g\kappa_c,\phi)$ with a single overdispersion $\phi$
estimated from the ambient residuals ($\phi\!\to\!0$ recovers the Poisson ambient test). One knob,
fast, auto-adapting Poisson$\leftrightarrow$NB. Then I benchmarked it head-to-head against the plain
ambient test and fishash, on (i) the authors' simulator across the **Simpson $\times$ overdispersion**
grid and (ii) the **real barnyard** ground truth.

![Realized FDR (top, dashed = nominal 5%) and recall (bottom) across regimes. fishash (green) is the
only method that controls FDR *and* keeps high recall everywhere. The plain ambient test (grey) fails
FDR in every regime. The NB candidate is bracketed by two failure modes: a global $\phi$ (pink)
controls FDR but halves recall; a robust $\phi$ (orange) restores recall but breaks FDR.](results/benchmark_update/build_vs_adopt.png)

**The result is decisive — and negative for "build."**

- **The plain ambient test does not control FDR** on any simulator regime (realized FDR 0.06–0.40).
  Its apparent wins elsewhere come from forgiving per-cell metrics on high-signal data, not rigorous
  per-guide FDR.
- **fishash controls FDR at recall $\approx$ 0.95 across Simpson and overdispersion**, the only method
  in the good corner of the trade-off. (Its lone simulator wobble — pure overdispersion, 1/5 reps —
  does **not** appear on real overdispersed data: see below.)
- **The NB candidate is dominated.** A single global overdispersion parameter is caught between
  over-conservatism (global $\phi$ → FDR controlled but recall ≈ 0.4) and anti-conservatism (robust
  $\phi$ → recall ≈ 0.95 but FDR ≈ 0.1–0.2). No tuning of a plug-in $\phi$ attains both; fishash's
  *conditional* contingency test calibrates without estimating $\phi$ at all.

**Real-data confirmation (barnyard, Table-2 accuracy):**

| | CROP 0hr | CROP 72hr | DC 0hr | DC 72hr | **mean** |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| ambient (Poisson) | 0.935 | 0.964 | 0.953 | 0.948 | **0.950** |
| fishash | 0.909 | 0.949 | **0.957** | **0.953** | **0.942** |
| NB candidate | 0.489 | 0.544 | 0.000 | 0.101 | **0.284** |

The candidate **collapses on real data** (and is worst exactly on overdispersed direct-capture, 0.00/0.10).
The simple ambient test and fishash are essentially tied (0.950 vs 0.942), and **fishash wins the two
direct-capture (overdispersed) samples** — its simulator overdispersion wobble does not manifest on real
overdispersed data.

# The canonical improvement: decontaminate the *cell* margin

The marginal-NB failure above was instructive: it failed because a **marginal** test needs the absolute
rate to be exactly right, whereas fishash's **conditional** (contingency) test self-calibrates. So the
right move is to improve *inside* the conditional framework. Reading fishash's source shows a clean,
asymmetric gap: **fishash's Simpson correction decontaminates the "other cells" but uses the raw
library size `N_{:,c}` as the focal cell's exposure (the hypergeometric draws) — it never decontaminates
the "other guides in the focal cell."** But our cross-dataset finding is exactly that `N_{:,c}` is the
wrong exposure (library ≠ ambient depth). The **canonical, symmetric completion** is to decontaminate
that entry too, so the cell margin becomes the **ambient depth**, not the library.

I implemented this as a modular contingency test (`scripts/contingency_method.R`). With the observed
cell margin it **reproduces fishash exactly** (identical assignments); swapping to the ambient-depth
margin is a clean one-factor ablation.

![The depth fix (ambient-depth cell margin) vs. fishash across MOI. As MOI rises, fishash loses recall
(co-occurring guides in a cell with one dominant integration get over-penalized by the inflated library
margin); the depth fix recovers it, at controlled FDR.](results/benchmark_update/depth_fix.png)

**This is a genuine, motivated, performant win — and it targets fishash's *documented* weak spot.**

- **Simulations:** the depth fix **beats fishash for MOI ≥ 1** (per-guide F1 0.96 / 0.93 / 0.89 at MOI
  1 / 3 / 5 vs fishash 0.96 / 0.89 / 0.82), **ties at low MOI**, FDR controlled throughout. fishash's own
  Fig. 6 shows it loses at MOI ≥ 1 — we now have the mechanism (contaminated cell margin) and the fix.
- **Real barnyard:** the depth fix **ties fishash (0.937 vs 0.942, no regression)**, including on the
  overdispersed direct-capture samples — it doesn't hurt where the high-MOI advantage doesn't apply.

**The overdispersion tail — an honest negative.** I also built the canonical overdispersed *conditional*
tail (NB, the stable Poisson-limit of the beta-binomial; φ estimated from the noise). On the simulator
it **works** — it rescues FDR under overdispersion (0.199 → 0.054 at controlled recall). But on **real
barnyard it collapses (Table-2 0.02)**: the φ estimator that I tuned on the simulator produces a
wildly wrong dispersion on real data, exactly as the standalone marginal NB did. **φ estimation is the
genuinely hard, non-robust part** — which is *why* fishash's plain equidispersed hypergeometric is a
wise choice, and it already handles real overdispersed (direct-capture) data well. So: **do not deploy
the overdispersion tail; keep the hypergeometric.** Overdispersion remains open, but low-value (fishash
is fine on real overdispersed data).

# Recommendation

**Adopt fishash's contingency core (Fisher test + Simpson correction + Guo–Sarkar FDR), and apply our
one canonical improvement — decontaminate the cell margin (use ambient depth, not library size).** This
is the "method of our own" that holds up: it is the *symmetric completion* of fishash's own
decontamination, motivated directly by our cross-dataset depth finding, and it **beats fishash at high
MOI while tying everywhere else** (sims and real data) at controlled FDR. Do not ship the bare ambient
test as the flagship, do not pursue the from-scratch marginal NB, and do not deploy an overdispersion
tail (φ is not robustly estimable on real data). The evidence:

1. **Accuracy on real, unbiased ground truth:** fishash (0.942) $\approx$ ambient (0.950) on barnyard,
   and fishash *wins* the overdispersed direct-capture samples.
2. **Statistical calibration:** fishash is the only method that controls per-guide FDR across Simpson
   and overdispersion at high recall. The simple ambient test is **not FDR-calibrated** — a real
   liability for a flagship method supporting genome-scale inference.
3. **Speed/scale:** fishash runs in seconds at <1 GiB even at 80,000 guides — like the ambient test,
   unlike CLEANSER's MCMC.
4. **It is understood and reproduced:** we have independently verified its Simpson correction and FDR
   behavior; adopting it is not a black box.

**On "a method of our own."** The honest scientific finding is that the most natural from-scratch design
(decontaminated rank-1 mean + NB tail) is *dominated* by fishash, for a principled reason — a global
overdispersion parameter cannot simultaneously control FDR and preserve power, whereas conditioning
sidesteps the problem. So our contribution should be **on top of the contingency core, not a replacement
of it**:

- **A transparent re-derivation + reference implementation** of the contingency/Simpson method (we have
  most of the understanding and reproduction already) — valuable for the SCEPTRE3 ecosystem and not a
  black-box dependency.
- **Targeted, principled improvements** to fishash's acknowledged soft spots: the conservatism of the
  GS correction (adaptive $\pi_0$), and the rank-1-vs-rank-2 noise mismatch. These are incremental and
  defensible.
- The **simple ambient test remains a justified fast default** for high-signal data and for QC/triage —
  but labeled as such, not as the rigorous method.

**Honest caveats.** (i) The simulator is fishash's own and may favor its test; but the barnyard is real
and unbiased and still ranks fishash $\approx$ ambient $\gg$ NB. (ii) I tested one novel design family
(global-$\phi$ NB tail). A depth-stratified **empirical-null** tail is the one untested idea, but these
results (plug-in overdispersion is fragile; fishash already handles real overdispersed data) make it low
expected value. (iii) All sim metrics are per-guide FDR/recall; the barnyard is per-cell Table-2 — the
two agree on the ranking, which is reassuring.
